books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, A. Migrations and New Communities in the Age of the Market Revolution

primary_sources: John L. O'Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity” (1839)

stimulus.text: John L. O’Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, November 1839: “American patriotism is not of soil; we are not aborigines, nor of ancestry, for we are of all nations; but it is essentially personal enfranchisement, for ‘where liberty dwells,’ said Franklin, the sage of the Revolution, ‘there is my country.’” O’Sullivan also wrote that “the nation of many nations is destined to manifest to mankind the excellence of divine principles.”
stimulus.source_note: John L. O'Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, vol. 6, no. 23 (November 1839), pp. 426-430. Verbatim quotations verified against Wikisource. Survivor rewrite of pr25e-test1-q18: new stimulus passage, new stem, new options, new explanations.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: O'Sullivan argues that American patriotism rests on

options.text: the soil where a person was born
options.misconception: O'Sullivan says patriotism is “not of soil.”

options.text: descent from the first English settlers
options.misconception: O'Sullivan says Americans are “not of ancestry, for we are of all nations.”

options.text: liberty and personal enfranchisement, not birthplace or ancestry
loyalty to the state where a person lives
options.misconception: O'Sullivan roots patriotism in liberty itself, quoting Franklin, not in loyalty to one state.

rationales.A: O'Sullivan's first words deny it: patriotism is “not of soil.” Birthplace is not his ground.
rationales.B: He denies ancestry too: Americans are “not of ancestry, for we are of all nations.” Descent is not his ground either.
rationales.C: O'Sullivan writes that American patriotism is “not of soil” and “not of ancestry, for we are of all nations.” What binds Americans is liberty: “where liberty dwells, there is my country.”
rationales.D: Franklin's line makes the country wherever liberty dwells, not one state. O'Sullivan's patriotism crosses state lines.
rationales.general:
1. Cross out what he denies. Not soil, not ancestry.
2. Keep what he affirms. Patriotism is personal enfranchisement.
3. Hear the Franklin quote. Where liberty dwells, there is my country.
Background: O'Sullivan wrote in 1839, as immigration was rising and expansion was carrying Americans west.
Remember: when a writer says what something is not, the denial is part of the claim.
